questions.prompt: What is an Architecture Review Board (ARB), as this course defines it?
options: A standing or convened group with the authority to approve, condition, or reject a proposed architecture before significant build investment
A tool that automatically scans code for security vulnerabilities
An informal hallway conversation between two architects about a design
A compliance checklist with no actual authority to block a design
A single senior architect who has final say with no other reviewers involved
A scheduled meeting that only occurs after a system has already been built
questions.explain: An ARB is a deliberately convened group with defined evaluators and real authority to approve, condition, or reject a design before significant engineering investment is committed to it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D describes a process with no real teeth -- a genuine ARB specifically carries actual authority to block or condition a design, which is exactly what separates it from a checklist that only produces opinions nobody has to act on.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 1, which of these is one of the evaluation domains a well-run ARB systematically checks a design against?
options: The presenter's personal popularity
Scalability and performance
The font used in the presentation slides
Whether the architect has worked at the company the longest
questions.explain: Lesson 1 lists requirements traceability, scalability and performance, security, integration, data model and quality, governance and maintainability, and risk/tradeoffs as the systematic evaluation domains -- personal popularity and tenure have no place in a real board's evaluation.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the difference between an ARB and an informal hallway design review, per Lesson 1.
options: An ARB is convened deliberately, not ad hoc
An ARB has defined evaluators who aren't personally invested in the specific design
An ARB produces a documented outcome
An ARB carries no real authority beyond offering opinions
A hallway review carries the same formal blocking authority as an ARB
questions.explain: An ARB is deliberately convened, staffed with independent evaluators, and produces a documented outcome with real blocking authority -- a hallway conversation, however valuable, has none of these formal properties.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 2, why should an architecture presentation lead with the business problem and constraints before showing any diagram?
options: Because diagrams are not allowed in review boards
Because it prevents reviewers from spending early attention reverse-engineering the business context from technical choices, instead of evaluating the design
Because boards never ask about business context
Because it allows the presenter to skip discussing requirements entirely
questions.explain: Reviewers who don't yet know the requirements spend early minutes inferring business context from technical choices -- minutes better spent evaluating the design. Leading with the problem gives every later decision an already-understood justification.

questions.prompt: Put these five sections of an architecture review presentation in the order Lesson 3 recommends.
questions.explain: The structure runs context/requirements, high-level architecture, deep dives on load-bearing decisions, tradeoffs and risks, then close and roadmap -- each section builds on the shared understanding the previous one established.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 4, why is a decision justified only by abstract 'best practice,' with no specific requirement behind it, the hardest to defend under questioning?
options: Because best practices are always technically wrong
Because there's nothing concrete to point back to when a reviewer asks what requirement actually demanded it
Because reviewers are not allowed to ask about best practices
Because best-practice decisions are never questioned by a board
questions.explain: Decisions tied to a specific stated requirement can be defended by simply restating that connection. A decision justified only by 'best practice' in the abstract has nothing concrete to point back to, making it the hardest to defend live.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lesson 5 to its meaning.
right: Asking a short question to resolve ambiguity in an objection before answering a guess
A challenge pushing a design to handle a scenario genuinely outside the stated requirements
A repeatable four-step pattern for responding to any technical objection
The expectation that a candidate may need to genuinely change their solution in response to a well-founded objection
questions.explain: Acknowledge-clarify-answer-check is the four-step response pattern. A scope-creep objection pushes beyond stated requirements. Defend-and-revise is the expectation that a solution may genuinely need to change under a well-founded objection. The clarify step specifically resolves ambiguity before answering a guess.

questions.prompt: A reviewer asks an ambiguous question where the two possible interpretations would lead to genuinely different designs. Per Lesson 6, what's the better move?
options: Silently pick one interpretation and answer as if it were the only one
Ask a clarifying question, since guessing wrong would waste real time building out the wrong branch
Refuse to answer the question at all
Ask a clarifying question about every small detail in the question, no matter how minor
questions.explain: When interpretations diverge into genuinely different designs, asking a clarifying question avoids wasting time on the wrong branch -- the failure mode to avoid is the opposite extreme of over-clarifying every minor detail.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Per Lesson 6, a ________ assumption is one significant enough that your answer would change meaningfully if it turned out to be wrong, and should always be stated out loud before answering.
questions.explain: A load-bearing assumption would change the answer significantly if wrong, so Lesson 6 says to state it explicitly -- distinct from an incidental assumption that doesn't need to be litigated out loud.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 7, why does the lesson recommend deciding on a small, consistent visual vocabulary before a live whiteboard session, rather than inventing conventions on the spot?
options: Because review boards require a single government-standard diagram notation
Because inventing conventions under pressure is a losing strategy, and consistency lets the board read the diagram far faster
Because only one shape is legally permitted per diagram
Because visual vocabulary has no bearing on how quickly a diagram can be read
questions.explain: Deciding on a small, practiced set of shapes and markings in advance avoids improvising notation under pressure, and consistent use lets the board read the diagram quickly instead of relearning the notation as it changes.

questions.prompt: Select every live-whiteboarding execution mistake Lesson 7 identifies, independent of whether the underlying design is sound.
options: Writing too small to be legible from where the board is sitting
Drawing the whole diagram in silence and narrating only at the end
Running out of planned space because the layout wasn't planned loosely in advance
Using a consistent shape for the same kind of component throughout the session
Erasing and redrawing repeatedly in a way that makes the final diagram hard to follow
questions.explain: Writing too small, narrating only at the end, running out of planned space, and excessive erasing/redrawing are all execution mistakes -- using a consistent shape for the same kind of component is a recommended practice, not a mistake.

questions.prompt: What does 'triage,' as Lesson 8 uses the term, mean when a presenter realizes they are running behind schedule?
options: Deciding what to cut or compress based on value, rather than rushing through every planned section equally
Immediately ending the presentation without finishing
Speeding up delivery of every section proportionally so nothing has to be cut
Asking the board to formally extend the time limit
Ignoring the clock entirely and continuing exactly as originally planned
Skipping straight to the Q&A phase without finishing the presentation
questions.explain: Triage means prioritizing the highest-value remaining content -- cutting or compressing lower-value sections -- rather than treating every section as equally important when time runs short.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes rushing proportionally through everything, which Lesson 8 specifically calls backwards: it compresses load-bearing content exactly as much as incidental content, instead of triaging deliberately by value.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 9, why does the lesson say self-correcting a mistake is almost always a better bet than hoping it goes unnoticed?
options: Because reviewers never notice inconsistencies in a presentation
Because an experienced panel is listening carefully, and being caught in an inconsistency you could have fixed yourself reads worse than catching it yourself
Because self-correction guarantees a passing outcome
Because panels are required to ignore any uncorrected mistake
questions.explain: Experienced reviewers are listening carefully as part of the job. Being caught in an inconsistency you could have corrected yourself reads worse than fixing it the moment you notice it -- self-correction signals you're tracking your own presentation.

questions.prompt: Match each reading-the-room concept from Lesson 10 to its meaning.
right: Multiple consecutive questions probing the same area, indicating real scrutiny regardless of panelists' expressions
Mistakenly treating a blank panelist expression as negative feedback and reacting defensively to it
A panel's deliberate practice of maintaining a flat expression to avoid signaling approval or disapproval
A reviewer writing something down right after a specific statement, often indicating it will resurface as a later question
questions.explain: Trained neutrality is the deliberate flat expression panels maintain. A note-taking cue is a reviewer writing something down right after a statement. Follow-up clustering is multiple questions probing the same area. Over-reading neutrality is mistakenly treating that flat expression as a bad sign.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 11, why is a full mock review simulation needed instead of only practicing the individual skills from Chapters 1 and 2 separately?
options: Because practicing individual skills in isolation is never useful
Because a real board demands all those skills simultaneously, under a single clock, rather than one at a time
Because full simulations are a formal requirement of every review board
Because individual skills can only be learned by first running a full simulation
questions.explain: The individual skills are easier to practice separately, which is why they were taught that way -- but a real board demands presenting, defending, handling ambiguity, and recovering from mistakes all at once, which only a full simulation actually rehearses.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the security-focused simulation objections covered in Lesson 12.
options: A strong answer names a specific mechanism, such as a role-based access model or an automated offboarding trigger, rather than a general assurance
'We'll encrypt it' fully answers any question about access control, logging, or breach response
A thorough security answer should be able to address prevention, detection, and response
Sustained questioning on one domain is a different test than a single question on that same topic
Encryption is never a legitimate or necessary security control
questions.explain: Strong answers name specific mechanisms and cover prevention, detection, and response; sustained domain pressure is genuinely different from a single question. Encryption is a real, necessary control, but offered alone it doesn't answer a question about who has access, what's logged, or breach response.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 13, what does a strong live answer to the synchronous-versus-asynchronous integration question typically do?
options: Picks whichever pattern is easiest to build and defends it as the only option
Names the actual business requirement that decides it, and reasons toward a possible hybrid rather than treating it as a strict either/or
Refuses to engage with the question since the choice is arbitrary
Always chooses asynchronous regardless of the stated business requirement
questions.explain: A strong answer ties the choice to the actual business requirement while naming the tradeoff of full dependency on an external vendor's uptime, often landing on a reasoned hybrid rather than picking one pattern with no middle ground.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ is the property that prevents a retried operation, such as a duplicate eligibility-check submission, from causing a duplicate effect.
questions.explain: Idempotency specifically prevents a retried operation from causing a duplicate effect -- Lesson 13's rehearsed objection asks what stops an automatic retry from submitting the same request twice, which an idempotency key addresses directly.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 14, why is domain-structured feedback more useful than a single overall pass/fail verdict?
options: Because it takes less time for a board to produce than an overall verdict
Because it tells you exactly where to focus next, using the same categories the board evaluated against, rather than leaving you to guess
Because domain-structured feedback is a legal requirement for every review board
Because it eliminates the need for any further practice afterward
questions.explain: A result broken down by the same evaluation domains the board used tells a candidate precisely where to focus next -- an undifferentiated pass/fail verdict throws away that most useful part of the result.

questions.prompt: Match each feedback example to whether Lesson 14 would call it a design gap or a performance gap.
left: "Your data model didn't account for returning customers across locations"
"You ran out of time before covering your tradeoffs"
"Your design never named a fallback for the eligibility API being down"
"You read your slides verbatim instead of explaining naturally"
questions.explain: A design gap means the solution itself needs to change (a missing consideration or control). A performance gap means the solution may have been fine, but presentation, pacing, or delivery fell short -- the two require different fixes.
